description: Focus Drills: neuroanatomy and clinical correlation, paediatric epilepsy syndromes, medication effects on the EEG, and the ACNS guidelines (2016 Guidelines 1-7, 2021 Critical Care EEG Terminology, 2015 cEEG consensus). Kept apart from the main question bank and served only on the drill page.

questions.stem: A right-handed man has a stroke. He understands what is said to him but speaks in slow, effortful fragments and is frustrated by it. His right face and arm are weak. Where is the lesion?
options: Left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area)
questions.explanation: Non-fluent speech with intact comprehension is Broca (expressive) aphasia. Broca area lies in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, just in front of the motor strip for the face and hand, which is why right face and arm weakness usually come with it. About 95% of right-handers are left-hemisphere dominant for language. Wernicke aphasia is fluent with poor comprehension; the right hemisphere is not dominant here; the angular gyrus gives alexia with agraphia.
questions.memoryAid: BROCA = BROKEN speech, front of the brain. The patient KNOWS it is broken, so they are frustrated.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient speaks fluently but in nonsense, with made-up words, does not follow commands and seems unaware of the problem. Which area is damaged?
questions.explanation: Fluent speech with paraphasias, poor comprehension and lack of awareness is Wernicke (receptive) aphasia from damage to the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, just behind the primary auditory cortex. There is usually no weakness because the motor strip is far away, though a superior quadrantanopia may occur.
questions.memoryAid: WERNICKE = WORDY, WRONG and WON'T understand. Wernicke is in the temporal lobe next to hearing: it is the 'listening' area.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient speaks fluently and understands well, but cannot repeat a sentence back. Which structure is most likely damaged?
questions.explanation: Conduction aphasia: fluent speech and good comprehension, but repetition fails because the arcuate fasciculus, the white matter bundle linking Wernicke (posterior) to Broca (anterior), is cut. The two language areas work, but the message cannot travel between them.
questions.memoryAid: CONDUCTION = can't COPY. The 'wire' (arcuate fasciculus) between the ear area and the mouth area is cut.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After a dominant parietal stroke a patient cannot name her fingers, confuses left and right, cannot write and cannot do simple sums. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: These four signs form Gerstmann syndrome, from damage to the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule. Non-dominant parietal damage instead produces neglect of the left side of space.
questions.memoryAid: Gerstmann = 'FALL': Finger agnosia, Acalculia, Left-right confusion, Lettering lost (agraphia).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After a right parietal stroke, a woman eats only the food on the right side of her plate, shaves only the right side of her face, and denies anything is wrong. What is this?
options: Left hemineglect from non-dominant parietal damage
Right homonymous hemianopia from occipital damage
questions.explanation: Neglect of the left side of space and the body, often with denial of illness (anosognosia), comes from damage to the non-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe. A hemianopia patient knows a field is missing and turns the head to compensate; a neglect patient behaves as if the left side does not exist.
questions.memoryAid: RIGHT parietal = the RIGHT side is all that's LEFT. The right hemisphere watches both sides; the left only watches the right, so right damage loses the left.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient has weakness of the left leg much more than the left arm, with apathy and urinary incontinence. Which artery is blocked?
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere, where the leg and foot are represented on the motor and sensory strips (the homunculus hangs upside down, legs over the top into the midline). Medial frontal damage also causes apathy (abulia) and incontinence. Signs are contralateral, so a left leg points to the right ACA.
questions.memoryAid: ACA = ANKLES (leg). MCA = MOUTH and ARM. PCA = PICTURES (vision).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which deficit pattern best fits a left middle cerebral artery stroke?
options: Right leg weakness greater than arm, abulia
Right face and arm weakness greater than leg, aphasia, eyes deviated to the left
Left face and arm weakness with left neglect
Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing only
questions.explanation: The MCA supplies the lateral convexity: the face and arm areas of the motor and sensory strips, language areas (in the dominant hemisphere) and the frontal eye field. A destructive lesion of the left frontal eye field lets the right one push the eyes toward the lesion (left). Leg weakness points to the ACA; isolated hemianopia to the PCA; left-sided signs to the right hemisphere.
questions.memoryAid: In a STROKE the eyes LOOK AT the lesion. In a SEIZURE the eyes LOOK AWAY from the focus.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient can write a paragraph but cannot read it back a minute later. Vision is lost in the right field. Which artery and structures are involved?
options: Left PCA: left occipital cortex and splenium of the corpus callosum
questions.explanation: Alexia without agraphia: the left occipital cortex is destroyed (right hemianopia) and the splenium is damaged, so what the intact right occipital lobe sees cannot cross to the left-hemisphere language areas. Writing is intact because the language and motor areas are fine. Both structures are supplied by the left posterior cerebral artery.
questions.memoryAid: Can WRITE but can't READ = the visual message can't CROSS the bridge (splenium). PCA = Pictures.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A hypertensive patient has pure weakness of the right face, arm and leg, equally, with no sensory loss, aphasia or field cut. A routine EEG is most likely to show what?
options: Continuous polymorphic delta over the left convexity
questions.explanation: Pure motor hemiparesis with face, arm and leg equally involved is a lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (lenticulostriate branches of the MCA). The lesion is small and deep, below the cortex, so the scalp EEG is often normal or shows only mild changes. Convexity cortex and white matter strokes give focal slowing.
questions.memoryAid: LACUNE = LITTLE and LOW (deep): the EEG often LOOKS normal. 'Pure motor, pure capsule.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Continuous, irregular (polymorphic) delta over one region, unchanged by eye opening or alerting, most strongly suggests a lesion in which location?
options: The thalamus on the opposite side
Subcortical white matter beneath that region
A purely superficial cortical gray matter lesion
questions.explanation: Continuous polymorphic delta activity is the classic sign of a structural lesion involving the subcortical white matter, which disconnects the overlying cortex from its thalamic inputs. Lesions confined to the cortical gray matter tend instead to reduce amplitude and faster activity, and deep midline lesions give intermittent, often bilateral, rhythmic delta.
questions.memoryAid: POLYMORPHIC delta = POOR white matter below. 'White matter cut = cortex drifts slow.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient's alpha rhythm blocks normally on the right when the eyes open, but persists on the left. What is this, and where is the lesion likely to be?
options: Bancaud phenomenon: a lesion on the right
A normal asymmetry of up to 50%
Bancaud phenomenon: a lesion on the left
questions.explanation: Failure of the alpha rhythm to attenuate on one side with eye opening or mental effort is the Bancaud phenomenon. The side that fails to react is abnormal, usually from a lesion in the parietal, temporal or occipital region of that hemisphere. Amplitude asymmetries are judged differently (the right is often slightly higher in normals); the key here is reactivity.
questions.memoryAid: BANCAUD = the side that won't BAN (block) the alpha is the BAD side.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Sleep spindles are consistently absent over the left hemisphere in an adult. Which structure is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Spindles are generated by thalamocortical circuits, paced by the thalamic reticular nucleus. A lesion of the thalamus (or the thalamocortical connections and cortex) on one side reduces spindles on that same side. Persistent unilateral spindle loss is abnormal at any age once spindles have developed.
questions.memoryAid: SPINDLES are SPUN by the THALAMUS, same side. 'No spindle on the left = look at the left thalamus.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An arch-shaped 9 Hz rhythm at C3 attenuates when the patient makes a fist with the right hand. What is it and where is it generated?
options: Alpha rhythm from the left occipital lobe
Wicket spikes from the left temporal lobe
Mu rhythm from the left sensorimotor (Rolandic) cortex
questions.explanation: Mu is an arciform 7-11 Hz rhythm over the central regions (C3, C4), generated in the sensorimotor cortex around the central sulcus. It blocks with movement (or the thought of movement) of the opposite limb, not with eye opening. Left-sided mu blocks with right-hand movement.
questions.memoryAid: MU = MOVE. Arches like the letter M. Block it by moving the OPPOSITE hand.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After a right craniotomy, a patient has higher-amplitude, sharper, faster activity over the right central region. What does this represent?
options: A breach rhythm from the skull defect
questions.explanation: A skull defect removes bone, which normally filters and attenuates high-frequency activity, so the activity under the defect is larger and sharper (breach rhythm). It often looks like mu and can contain sharply contoured waves. It is not epileptiform by itself, though true spikes can coexist and must be judged carefully.
questions.memoryAid: BREACH = BONE gone: the EEG is BIGGER and BRIGHTER (faster) over the hole.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A focal motor seizure starts in the right foot. Where would the focus most likely be?
options: Left parasagittal motor cortex, near Cz
Left lateral frontal lobe, near F7
questions.explanation: On the motor homunculus the foot and leg sit at the top of the precentral gyrus and dip into the interhemispheric fissure, close to the midline (Cz). The face is low and lateral (near F7/T3 regions). Motor control is crossed, so the right foot points to the left hemisphere. Parasagittal foci may show best at Cz and can be hard to lateralize.
questions.memoryAid: The homunculus HANGS upside down: FEET at the TOP (midline, Cz), FACE at the bottom (lateral).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During a temporal lobe seizure a patient has lip-smacking, fumbling movements of the left hand, and a stiff, twisted posture of the right arm. Which side is the seizure focus?
questions.explanation: Unilateral dystonic posturing of an arm is contralateral to the seizure focus. Manual automatisms (fumbling, picking) tend to involve the hand on the same side as the focus. Both clues point to the left.
questions.memoryAid: DYSTONIA is DISTANT (opposite side). AUTOMATISMS stay AT HOME (same side).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient talks normally throughout a complex partial seizure and has no language problem afterwards. Which lateralization is most likely?
questions.explanation: Preserved, understandable speech during a seizure points to a non-dominant focus. Postictal aphasia (word-finding or comprehension problems after the seizure) points to the dominant hemisphere.
questions.memoryAid: TALKS through it = the TALKING side is spared (non-dominant focus). Aphasia afterwards = the language side was hit.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient has a right third nerve palsy (eye down and out, dilated pupil) and weakness of the left arm and leg. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Crossed signs (a cranial nerve on one side, limb weakness on the other) mean the brainstem. The third nerve leaves the front of the midbrain next to the cerebral peduncle, which carries corticospinal fibres that have not yet crossed. A right ventral midbrain lesion gives a right III palsy and left hemiparesis (Weber syndrome).
questions.memoryAid: CROSSED signs = BRAINSTEM. The nerve tells you the LEVEL and the SIDE (III = midbrain).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After a basilar artery stroke, a patient cannot move or speak but blinks and looks up on command. What will the EEG most likely show?
options: Alpha coma that does not react
A normal, reactive posterior alpha rhythm
questions.explanation: This is locked-in syndrome from a lesion of the ventral pons that cuts the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts but spares the reticular activating system and the cortex. The patient is fully awake and aware, so the EEG is usually normal with a reactive alpha rhythm. The EEG helps tell locked-in from coma.
questions.memoryAid: LOCKED IN = the person is still IN there, and so is the ALPHA. Vertical eye movements are the only way out.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After cardiac arrest, a comatose patient's EEG shows diffuse, frontally prominent alpha-frequency activity that does not change with stimulation. What does this usually indicate?
options: Alpha coma, usually a poor prognosis after hypoxia
questions.explanation: Alpha coma is unreactive alpha-frequency activity in a comatose patient, often diffuse or frontally predominant after hypoxic-ischemic injury, and it usually carries a poor prognosis. It differs from normal alpha by its distribution and lack of reactivity. Drug-induced alpha coma can be reversible, so medications must always be considered.
questions.memoryAid: ALPHA in COMA that won't react = ALARM. Normal alpha is POSTERIOR and REACTIVE.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Generalized sharp-wave complexes repeating about once per second, with rapidly progressive dementia and startle myoclonus, suggest which disease?
questions.explanation: Periodic sharp-wave complexes at about 0.5-2 Hz (typically near 1 Hz) with rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus are characteristic of sporadic CJD, a prion disease. SSPE complexes repeat far more slowly (every 4-15 s). HSV gives temporal lateralized periodic discharges. Huntington disease gives a low-voltage record.
questions.memoryAid: CJD ticks like a CLOCK: about 1 per second. 'Creutzfeldt-Jakob = Clock-like Jerks.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with a history of measles has declining school performance and periodic jerks. The EEG shows high-voltage complexes repeating every 5-10 seconds. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: SSPE is a late complication of measles. Its periodic complexes (Radermecker complexes) are high-voltage, stereotyped slow-wave complexes repeating every 4-15 seconds, often with each jerk. That long interval separates it from CJD (about 1 per second).
questions.memoryAid: SSPE = SLOW, SPACED Periodic complexes. Measles years ago, Spaced complexes now.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A febrile, confused adult has olfactory hallucinations and a temporal lobe signal on MRI. The EEG shows lateralized periodic discharges over the left temporal region. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus has a predilection for the mesial temporal and orbitofrontal lobes. Lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs, formerly PLEDs) over a temporal region in an encephalitic patient strongly suggest HSV and should prompt urgent acyclovir. Metabolic encephalopathy gives generalized patterns such as triphasic waves.
questions.memoryAid: HSV HITS the TEMPORAL lobe and makes LPDs: 'Herpes = Hippocampus + LPDs.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During an eye blink, why do Fp1 and Fp2 become positive?
options: The retina moves toward Fp1 and Fp2
The eyelid muscles generate a positive spike
The positive cornea rolls upward toward Fp1 and Fp2 (Bell phenomenon)
questions.explanation: The eye is a dipole: the cornea is positive relative to the retina. On closing the lids the eyes roll upward (Bell phenomenon), bringing the positive cornea toward the frontopolar electrodes. In a bipolar chain starting Fp1-F3, a positive Fp1 is the first input going positive, which by convention gives a downward deflection.
questions.memoryAid: CORNEA is POSITIVE. Eyes roll UP on a blink, so the electrode they roll toward goes POSITIVE.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient looks to the left. Which pattern appears at F7 and F8?
questions.explanation: Looking left brings the positive left cornea toward F7 and moves the negative right retina toward F8. The result is opposite-phase deflections at F7 and F8, which is how lateral eye movements are recognised and separated from cerebral activity.
questions.memoryAid: The electrode the eyes LOOK TOWARD goes POSITIVE (cornea leads the way).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A drowsy, confused patient's EEG shows bifrontal rhythmic 2 Hz delta that comes and goes, with a relatively preserved background between runs. Besides metabolic encephalopathy, what else classically produces it?
options: Raised intracranial pressure or a deep midline lesion
questions.explanation: Frontal intermittent rhythmic delta (now called frontally predominant GRDA) is non-specific. It appears with metabolic and toxic encephalopathy and with raised intracranial pressure or deep midline or posterior fossa lesions that disturb diencephalic and brainstem projections. It is not a sign of a focal cortical lesion. The link with deep midline lesions and raised pressure is classical but weak; today it is seen far more often in toxic-metabolic states.
questions.memoryAid: FIRDA = FAR away lesion (deep or pressure), not under the electrode. 'Frontal, Intermittent, Remote cause.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient with drop attacks undergoes surgery that cuts the main commissure between the hemispheres. What is the procedure and why does it help?
options: Hemispherectomy: it removes a whole hemisphere
Corpus callosotomy: it limits spread of seizures between hemispheres
Temporal lobectomy: it removes the hippocampus
questions.explanation: Corpus callosotomy divides the corpus callosum, the largest commissure, which reduces rapid bilateral spread of seizures and especially helps atonic drop attacks. It is palliative rather than curative.
questions.memoryAid: CALLOSOTOMY stops the CROSSING: no crossing = no sudden DROP.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Postictal weakness of the right arm lasts several hours after a seizure. What does it suggest?
options: Todd paralysis: the seizure arose in the left hemisphere
Todd paralysis: the seizure arose in the right hemisphere
questions.explanation: Todd paralysis is temporary postictal weakness contralateral to the seizure focus, lasting minutes to (rarely) a day or two. It is a useful lateralizing sign. A deficit that does not resolve needs imaging to exclude a structural cause.
questions.memoryAid: TODD = TEMPORARY, opposite side. The tired (exhausted) cortex controls the weak side.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Where would you expect the clearest scalp evidence of a left mesial temporal (hippocampal) focus?
options: Anterior temporal electrodes (F7, T3, and T1 or sphenoidal if used)
questions.explanation: Mesial temporal discharges project to the basal and anterior temporal surface, so they are best seen at the anterior temporal electrodes (F7/T3 in the 10-20 system; F7 sits over the anterior temporal region), and better still at T1/T2 or sphenoidal electrodes placed closer to the mesial temporal lobe.
questions.memoryAid: HIPPOCAMPUS hides LOW and DEEP: look LOW and FRONT on the temporal chain (F7, T1, sphenoidal).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A frontal lobe seizure is most typical in which description?
options: Long staring spell with lip-smacking and long confusion afterwards
Flashing coloured lights in one visual field
Rising stomach feeling and deja vu
Brief, often nocturnal, with wild thrashing movements and quick recovery
questions.explanation: Frontal lobe seizures are typically brief (under a minute), cluster at night out of sleep, include bizarre hypermotor movements (bicycling, thrashing) and have little postictal confusion. They are often mistaken for psychogenic events, and the scalp EEG may be obscured by movement or show little. Staring with automatisms and long confusion fits temporal; flashes fit occipital; epigastric aura and deja vu fit mesial temporal.
questions.memoryAid: FRONTAL = FAST, FRANTIC and at NIGHT. 'Short, sleepy-time, and strange.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old has clusters of sudden flexion of the trunk and arms on waking, and has stopped smiling and babbling. What is the expected interictal EEG?
questions.explanation: Infantile spasms in clusters (often on waking), developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia make up West syndrome (infantile epileptic spasms syndrome), usually starting at about 3-12 months. Hypsarrhythmia is very high-voltage (often over 200 µV), chaotic slow activity with multifocal spikes and poor organisation.
questions.memoryAid: WEST = 'SHR': Spasms, Hypsarrhythmia, Regression. 'Wake-up clusters in a baby.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During an infantile spasm, which EEG change is most characteristic?
options: A generalized slow wave followed by abrupt attenuation (electrodecremental response)
questions.explanation: The ictal correlate of a spasm is typically a high-voltage generalized slow wave, sometimes with superimposed fast activity, followed by an electrodecremental response: sudden flattening of the background for a second or more. Hypsarrhythmia is the interictal background.
questions.memoryAid: SPASM = SLOW wave then SILENCE (decrement).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which genetic condition is a classic cause of infantile spasms, and which drug is especially effective for spasms in that condition?
questions.explanation: Tuberous sclerosis complex is one of the commonest identifiable causes of infantile spasms (hypoxic-ischaemic injury is the commonest overall), and vigabatrin is first-line for spasms in TSC. Vigabatrin can cause permanent visual field constriction, so vision is monitored. ACTH or high-dose steroids are first-line for most other causes.
questions.memoryAid: TSC → VIGABATRIN. 'Tubers need V.' Watch the VISUAL fields with Vigabatrin.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with developmental delay has tonic seizures in sleep, drop attacks and atypical absences. Which EEG pattern is expected?
options: Slow spike-and-wave at about 1.5-2.5 Hz, with paroxysmal fast activity in sleep
3 Hz spike-and-wave with a normal background
questions.explanation: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: multiple seizure types (tonic seizures, especially in sleep, atonic drops and atypical absences), cognitive impairment, and slow spike-and-wave below 2.5 Hz on a slow background. Bursts of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (about 10-25 Hz) in sleep accompany tonic seizures. Onset is usually 1-8 years, and some cases evolve from West syndrome.
questions.memoryAid: LGS = LESS than 2.5 Hz, LOTS of seizure types, and it often GROWS from West. 'Tonic in sleep, fast in sleep.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A healthy 7-year-old has dozens of brief staring spells a day; hyperventilation provokes one in the lab. What is the expected EEG and first-line drug?
questions.explanation: Childhood absence epilepsy: typically 4-10 years, many absences a day lasting about 10 seconds, abrupt start and stop, provoked by hyperventilation, with regular 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave on a normal background. Ethosuximide is first-line for absences alone (valproate also works but has more side effects). Carbamazepine can worsen absences.
questions.memoryAid: THREE Hz, THREE syllables: 'ab-sen-ces'. 'HV-provoked, Hundreds a day, ethoSUXimide SUCKS out absences.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 15-year-old drops her cup in the morning because of arm jerks, especially after late nights, and once had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which EEG fits?
options: 3 Hz spike-and-wave with a slow background
questions.explanation: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: onset usually 12-18 years, myoclonic jerks shortly after waking, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, sometimes absences; provoked by sleep deprivation and alcohol. EEG: generalized polyspike-and-wave at about 4-6 Hz on a normal background, often with a photoparoxysmal response. It is usually lifelong. Valproate or levetiracetam are used; carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonus.
questions.memoryAid: JME = Jerks in the Morning, Early; 'Coffee cup flies.' POLYspikes, PHOTOsensitive, Party (sleep loss, alcohol) triggers.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An 8-year-old has seizures from sleep with twitching of one side of the face, drooling and inability to speak but is aware. What does the EEG show and what is the outlook?
options: Normal EEG; this is not epilepsy
Sleep-activated centrotemporal spikes; remits by mid-adolescence
questions.explanation: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (benign Rolandic epilepsy): onset about 4-12 years, nocturnal focal seizures of the face and throat with drooling and speech arrest, awareness often kept. EEG: high-amplitude diphasic centrotemporal spikes, greatly increased in sleep, often with a horizontal dipole (frontal positivity). It remits by about age 16. Many children need no treatment.
questions.memoryAid: ROLANDIC = 'FACE, DROOL, can't TALK, at NIGHT, and it GOES AWAY.' Spikes sit at C3/T3 or C4/T4.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has a prolonged nocturnal episode of vomiting, pallor and eye deviation, then becomes unresponsive. The EEG shows occipital (and sometimes multifocal) spikes. What is the syndrome?
options: Panayiotopoulos syndrome (self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures)
questions.explanation: Panayiotopoulos syndrome begins at about 3-6 years with autonomic seizures (vomiting, pallor, sweating, pupil changes), eye deviation and often long duration (autonomic status). The EEG shows occipital or multifocal spikes, often shifting location. The outlook is excellent. The Gastaut type affects older children with visual hallucinations and headache.
questions.memoryAid: PANAYIOTOPOULOS = PUKING Preschooler (autonomic). Long name, long seizures, but good outcome.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has brief seizures that start with coloured circles in one visual field, followed by headache. Occipital spikes disappear when the eyes open. What is the syndrome?
questions.explanation: Childhood occipital visual epilepsy (Gastaut type) starts later (about 8-9 years) with brief elementary visual hallucinations and frequent postictal headache, so it is easily mistaken for migraine. Occipital spikes are blocked by eye opening and appear with eye closure (fixation-off sensitivity).
questions.memoryAid: GASTAUT = GLOWING circles, then a GRUMBLING headache. Older child, visual, brief.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 5-year-old who spoke normally gradually stops understanding speech and then stops talking. Hearing tests are normal. Sleep EEG shows near-continuous temporal spike-and-wave. What is this?
questions.explanation: Landau-Kleffner syndrome is acquired epileptic aphasia (verbal auditory agnosia) in a previously normal child, usually 3-7 years. Spike-and-wave is markedly activated in NREM sleep, often temporal and sometimes near-continuous (spike-wave activation in sleep). Seizures can be few. A sleep EEG is essential because the awake record can look nearly normal.
questions.memoryAid: LKS = LOST KID'S SPEECH. Always record SLEEP.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-and-wave activation in sleep (formerly ESES/CSWS), what is the key EEG finding?
options: Near-continuous spike-and-wave during NREM sleep, with cognitive regression
Normal sleep with awake 3 Hz spike-and-wave
questions.explanation: The hallmark is marked activation of spike-and-wave in NREM sleep, classically occupying most of slow sleep (historically 85% or more), together with neurocognitive regression. Spike-wave falls in REM and wakefulness. Landau-Kleffner syndrome is the language-predominant form.
questions.memoryAid: ESES = Electrical Status in Slow Sleep: 'Spikes take over the Slow sleep, Skills slip.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A previously normal 6-month-old has a long one-sided seizure with fever, then more prolonged febrile seizures; by age 2 she has myoclonus and developmental slowing. Which gene and drug class are key?
options: SCN1A; avoid sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine and lamotrigine
questions.explanation: Dravet syndrome: onset in the first year with prolonged, often hemiclonic febrile seizures, then multiple seizure types and developmental slowing. Most cases have an SCN1A variant. The early EEG is often normal. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin) can worsen seizures.
questions.memoryAid: DRAVET: 'DON'T give the SODIUM blockers' (SCN1A is a SODIUM channel). Fever + long seizures in the first year.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which description is a simple febrile seizure?
options: A generalized seizure under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, in a child aged 6 months to 5 years
Three seizures in one day with fever
A seizure with fever in a 9-year-old
questions.explanation: Simple febrile seizures are generalized, last under 15 minutes and do not recur within 24 hours, in children about 6 months to 5 years old. Focal features, duration of 15 minutes or more, or recurrence within 24 hours make it complex. An EEG is not routinely needed after a simple febrile seizure.
questions.memoryAid: SIMPLE = 'GENERAL, SHORT, ONCE' (under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A newborn in the first weeks of life has frequent tonic spasms. The EEG shows burst suppression awake and asleep. What syndrome is this?
options: Early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara syndrome)
questions.explanation: Ohtahara syndrome (now within early infantile DEE) begins in the first weeks to 3 months with tonic spasms and a burst-suppression pattern present in both waking and sleep. It is often structural or genetic (for example STXBP1, KCNQ2) and may evolve to West syndrome. Early myoclonic encephalopathy, the other classic form, has erratic myoclonus, is often metabolic, and its burst suppression is enhanced in sleep.
questions.memoryAid: OHTAHARA = 'OH so early': TONIC spasms, BURST SUPPRESSION all the time. Later it can head WEST.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A girl developed normally until about 12 months, then lost hand skills and speech and now makes repetitive hand-wringing movements. Which gene is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: Rett syndrome mainly affects girls, from MECP2 variants on the X chromosome. After apparently normal early development, there is regression with loss of purposeful hand use and speech, stereotyped hand-wringing, breathing irregularities and often seizures. The EEG shows background slowing and often centrotemporal spikes.
questions.memoryAid: RETT = girls who WRING their hands. 'MECP2 = Mostly girls, Erasing hand skills.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A happy, frequently laughing child with severe speech impairment, jerky ataxic gait and seizures has high-amplitude 2-3 Hz frontal delta with spikes. What is the syndrome?
questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome (loss of maternal UBE3A on chromosome 15q11-13) causes a happy, excitable demeanour, absent speech, ataxia and seizures. Characteristic EEG patterns include high-amplitude rhythmic 2-3 Hz delta with spikes (often frontally predominant), rhythmic 4-6 Hz theta, and posterior spikes with 3-4 Hz activity on eye closure.
questions.memoryAid: ANGELMAN = happy ANGEL with BIG delta. 'Laughing, ataxic, no speech, huge slow waves.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A child has a port-wine stain over the forehead and upper eyelid and seizures. What is typical on the EEG over the affected hemisphere?
options: Increased fast activity like a breach rhythm
Reduced amplitude (attenuation), sometimes with epileptiform activity
questions.explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome links a facial port-wine stain (V1 distribution) with a leptomeningeal angioma, cortical calcification and atrophy on the same side. The EEG typically shows reduced amplitude and slowing over the affected hemisphere, with epileptiform discharges.
questions.memoryAid: STURGE-WEBER = STAIN on the face, SUPPRESSED EEG on the same side.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has persistent focal motor seizures of the left hand that do not stop, worsening left-sided weakness and right hemisphere atrophy on serial MRI. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rasmussen encephalitis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammation of one hemisphere in childhood. It causes drug-resistant focal seizures, often epilepsia partialis continua (continuous focal motor seizures), progressive hemiparesis and progressive hemispheric atrophy. The EEG shows slowing and epileptiform activity over the affected hemisphere. Hemispheric surgery is often needed.
questions.memoryAid: RASMUSSEN = ONE hemisphere RUSTS away: continuous jerking (EPC) and growing weakness.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A child has brief seizures of laughter without mirth and early puberty. Where is the lesion?
questions.explanation: Gelastic (laughing) seizures with central precocious puberty point to a hypothalamic hamartoma. The scalp EEG is often normal or non-specific because the lesion is deep; it may show generalized or frontotemporal discharges as the epilepsy progresses.
questions.memoryAid: HAMARTOMA = HA-HA plus early hormones (puberty).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A newborn with a family history of neonatal seizures has seizures from day 2-3 of life that remit within weeks to months; development is normal. Which gene is classically involved?
questions.explanation: Self-limited (benign) familial neonatal epilepsy is usually caused by KCNQ2 (less often KCNQ3) potassium channel variants. Seizures start around days 2-7 and remit within weeks to months (usually by 6 months), with normal development in most. KCNQ2 variants can also cause a severe early-onset encephalopathy.
questions.memoryAid: KCNQ2 = 'K for Kin' (family) and K for potassium. Day 2-3, gone by months.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How does hypsarrhythmia typically change in sleep?
options: It is unchanged in all states
It fragments into bursts in NREM sleep and often lessens or disappears in REM
It appears only in wakefulness and not in sleep
questions.explanation: In NREM sleep hypsarrhythmia often becomes more synchronous and fragmented, with bursts separated by lower-voltage periods (a modified pattern). In REM sleep it often lessens or disappears. Spasms cluster on waking, so recording sleep and the wake-up period is useful.
questions.memoryAid: HYPS breaks into PIECES in NREM and RESTS in REM.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A normally developing 3-year-old boy suddenly has many drop attacks with brief myoclonic jerks. The EEG shows generalized 2-3 Hz spike- and polyspike-and-wave with parasagittal 4-7 Hz theta. Which syndrome is likely?
questions.explanation: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome) typically starts at about 2-5 years in previously normal children, more often boys, with myoclonic-atonic drops. The EEG shows generalized 2-6 Hz spike- and polyspike-and-wave and often rhythmic 4-7 Hz parasagittal theta. Unlike LGS, tonic seizures are not prominent early and development was normal before onset.
questions.memoryAid: DOOSE = DROPS in a NORMAL toddler boy. LGS = tonic seizures, delay, slow spike-wave.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which feature best separates Lennox-Gastaut syndrome from childhood absence epilepsy?
options: Slow spike-and-wave under 2.5 Hz with a slow background and cognitive impairment
questions.explanation: Both can have staring spells and generalized discharges. CAE has 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background in a normally developing child, strongly provoked by hyperventilation. LGS has slower (under 2.5 Hz) spike-and-wave on a slow background, multiple seizure types (especially tonic) and cognitive impairment.
questions.memoryAid: 3 Hz and HAPPY (normal kid) = CAE. UNDER 2.5 Hz and STRUGGLING = LGS.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A toddler cries hard after a minor fall, turns blue, goes limp and briefly stiffens. The EEG during an event shows slowing then flattening without spikes. What is this?
questions.explanation: Breath-holding spells are triggered by crying, pain or frustration, peak at 6-18 months, and are non-epileptic. Reduced brain oxygen causes EEG slowing and then flattening, sometimes with brief stiffening or jerks (an anoxic seizure), but no epileptiform discharges. They are linked with iron-deficiency anaemia.
questions.memoryAid: BREATH-HOLDING = TRIGGER first (cry), then COLOUR change, then the EEG goes SLOW then FLAT, no spikes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 13-year-old has absences a few times a week (less often than a younger child would) and occasional tonic-clonic seizures on waking. EEG shows generalized 3-4 Hz spike-and-wave, sometimes with polyspikes. Which syndrome?
questions.explanation: Juvenile absence epilepsy begins around 9-13 years (range about 8-20). Absences are less frequent but often longer than in CAE, generalized tonic-clonic seizures are common, and the spike-and-wave is often slightly faster (3-4 Hz) with polyspikes. It tends to be lifelong, whereas CAE usually remits.
questions.memoryAid: JUVENILE = fewer, longer absences, plus GTCs; slightly FASTER (3-4 Hz). CHILDHOOD = many short ones at 3 Hz.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has absences that do not respond to usual treatment, plus a movement disorder. CSF glucose is low. Which treatment is most specific?
questions.explanation: Early-onset absence epilepsy (before about 4 years), especially when drug-resistant or with movement disorders, should raise suspicion of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome (SLC2A1). Low CSF glucose relative to blood glucose supports it. The ketogenic diet provides ketones as an alternative brain fuel.
questions.memoryAid: GLUT1 = brain can't GET GLUCOSE in: feed it KETONES. 'Absences under 4: check the sugar door.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which drug can worsen typical absence and myoclonic seizures and should generally be avoided in childhood absence epilepsy and JME?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, vigabatrin, tiagabine) can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures in generalized epilepsies. Ethosuximide and valproate treat absences; valproate and levetiracetam treat myoclonic seizures.
questions.memoryAid: 'CARBAMAZEPINE CARRIES ABSENCES and JERKS further.' Sodium blockers are for FOCAL seizures.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, what dipole is typical of the spikes?
options: Vertical: negative at the vertex only
Radial: maximal at O1 and O2
questions.explanation: Centrotemporal spikes typically show a horizontal (tangential) dipole: negativity over the centrotemporal region and simultaneous positivity over the frontal region, because the generator lies in the lower Rolandic cortex oriented sideways. This is a supportive feature of the benign syndrome.
questions.memoryAid: ROLANDIC spike LIES DOWN sideways: negative at the side (C/T), positive at the front.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with jerks when startled and normal development shows brief myoclonic jerks with no EEG change. What is most likely?
options: A non-epileptic event such as benign myoclonus or exaggerated startle
questions.explanation: Epileptic myoclonus is time-locked to EEG discharges (spikes or polyspikes). Jerks without any EEG correlate in a normally developing child suggest a non-epileptic cause, such as benign sleep myoclonus, benign myoclonus of infancy or startle. Video-EEG with a muscle channel helps.
questions.memoryAid: A JERK with NO SPIKE in a thriving child is usually NOT epilepsy.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with tuberous sclerosis has focal seizures. Which EEG finding is most typical?
options: A normal record with no abnormalities
Multifocal epileptiform discharges matching the cortical tubers
questions.explanation: In tuberous sclerosis complex, cortical tubers are multiple epileptogenic lesions, so the EEG often shows multifocal (or focal) spikes and slowing. In infancy, many evolve to infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia. Associated features include ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas and cardiac rhabdomyomas.
questions.memoryAid: TUBERS are MANY, so the spikes are MANY (multifocal). 'Ash leaf on the skin, spikes all over the brain.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Shortly after a benzodiazepine is given, what is the most typical EEG change?
options: Increased diffuse beta activity, frontally predominant
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines produce increased beta activity (roughly 14-30 Hz, often about 20-25 Hz), most prominent over the frontal and central regions and symmetric. At higher doses they cause drowsiness, sleep and slowing. They also suppress epileptiform discharges and raise the photoparoxysmal threshold.
questions.memoryAid: BENZOS make BETA: 'B for B'. Front-loaded and symmetric.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient given lorazepam has prominent beta over the right hemisphere but almost none over the left. What does the asymmetry suggest?
options: Left hemisphere dysfunction or a fluid collection over the left (reduced beta)
questions.explanation: Drug-induced beta should be symmetric. Consistently less beta on one side points to that side: cortical dysfunction (for example a stroke) or something between cortex and electrode such as a subdural collection that damps fast activity. Increased fast activity on one side can mean a skull defect (breach rhythm) on that side.
questions.memoryAid: LESS BETA = the LESSER (damaged) side. 'Fast activity fades over damage and fluid.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient with refractory status epilepticus is placed in barbiturate coma. What EEG pattern is usually targeted?
questions.explanation: At anaesthetic doses barbiturates (pentobarbital, thiopental), like propofol and midazolam, produce burst suppression: bursts of activity alternating with suppressed background. In refractory status epilepticus, infusions are often titrated to seizure suppression or burst suppression. At lower doses barbiturates cause prominent beta activity.
questions.memoryAid: BARBITURATES: low dose = BETA, high dose = BURST suppression. 'Barbs go Beta, then Bursts.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Why are high blood levels of barbiturates or other sedatives a problem for confirming brain death by EEG?
options: They can suppress the EEG to apparent electrocerebral inactivity, which is reversible
They make the EEG impossible to record technically
questions.explanation: CNS depressant drugs (barbiturates, high-dose benzodiazepines, propofol and others) and hypothermia can produce a flat EEG that is reversible. Brain death evaluation requires excluding these confounders: drug levels must be cleared or below thresholds and core temperature normal.
questions.memoryAid: Before calling it FLAT, rule out the DRUGS and the COLD (sedatives and hypothermia).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient abruptly stops a long-term benzodiazepine, barbiturate or alcohol. What EEG and clinical risk increases?
options: Seizures and a photoparoxysmal response from withdrawal
questions.explanation: Abrupt withdrawal of GABA-ergic sedatives (benzodiazepines, barbiturates) or alcohol lowers the seizure threshold. Withdrawal seizures and photoparoxysmal responses can appear, and generalized discharges may emerge. Alcohol withdrawal seizures usually occur about 6-48 hours after the last drink.
questions.memoryAid: WITHDRAWAL WAKES the seizures: stopping a 'downer' fires the brain UP.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A child is given chloral hydrate for a sleep EEG. What change is expected?
options: Drowsiness and sleep, with at most a mild increase in beta
questions.explanation: Chloral hydrate is a sedative-hypnotic used for paediatric EEG sedation. It induces drowsiness and sleep with relatively little added beta (less than benzodiazepines or barbiturates) and preserves sleep architecture fairly well. It causes little suppression of epileptiform activity compared with benzodiazepines. Whether a child is sedated, and with what, is an institutional decision and must be documented.
questions.memoryAid: CHLORAL = CALM child, hardly any BETA. Always WRITE the sedative and time on the record.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which drug is used in some labs to activate interictal temporal spikes during an EEG?
questions.explanation: Methohexital, a short-acting barbiturate, can activate interictal epileptiform discharges, especially in temporal lobe epilepsy, at low doses. Most other barbiturates and benzodiazepines suppress discharges.
questions.memoryAid: METHOHEXITAL is the 'ME-THE-EXCITER': the odd barbiturate that BRINGS OUT spikes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the typical EEG effect of a therapeutic dose of phenytoin, and of toxicity?
options: Prominent burst suppression at therapeutic levels
Little change at therapeutic levels; slowing at toxic levels
questions.explanation: Phenytoin causes little background change at therapeutic levels. At toxic levels it causes diffuse slowing and clinical cerebellar signs (nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria), and very high levels can paradoxically increase seizures. Long-term use causes gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism.
questions.memoryAid: PHENYTOIN toxicity = the 'CEREBELLAR drunk': nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, plus slowing.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient on valproate becomes drowsy and confused. Ammonia is high and the EEG shows diffuse slowing with triphasic-like waves. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Valproate can cause hyperammonaemic encephalopathy even at normal drug levels, with lethargy, confusion and EEG slowing, sometimes with triphasic waves. Valproate otherwise changes the background little. Checking ammonia separates it from non-convulsive status.
questions.memoryAid: VALPROATE + confusion = check AMMONIA. 'V for VAPOUR of ammonia.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which antiepileptic drug is used mainly for absence seizures and works on T-type calcium channels in the thalamus?
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, which drive the 3 Hz thalamocortical rhythm of absence seizures. It is first-line for childhood absence epilepsy but does not protect against tonic-clonic seizures.
questions.memoryAid: ETHOSUXIMIDE = 'ETHO-SUCKS-out ABSENCES' via the thalamic T-type (T for Thalamus, T for Three Hz).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An infant with tuberous sclerosis starts vigabatrin. What adverse effect must be monitored?
questions.explanation: Vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase. It is first-line for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis but can cause permanent peripheral (concentric) visual field loss, so vision is monitored. It can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.
questions.memoryAid: VIGABATRIN = VISION. 'Vigabatrin shrinks the View.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: After ACTH treatment for infantile spasms is successful, what EEG change is hoped for?
questions.explanation: ACTH or high-dose oral steroids (and vigabatrin) aim for electroclinical response: cessation of spasms and resolution of hypsarrhythmia on a follow-up EEG, ideally including sleep. Persistent hypsarrhythmia means incomplete response.
questions.memoryAid: Treating WEST = the HYPS must go and the SPASMS must stop (both).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the typical EEG effect of tricyclic antidepressants?
options: Prominent burst suppression at usual doses
Increased theta and beta, reduced alpha; overdose causes slowing and seizures
questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants (for example amitriptyline, imipramine) increase theta and beta and reduce alpha. They lower the seizure threshold; in overdose they cause slowing, epileptiform discharges, seizures and cardiac arrhythmias.
questions.memoryAid: TRICYCLICS = TRIPLE trouble in overdose: SEIZURES, SLOWING and the HEART.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient on lithium becomes confused and tremulous. What EEG findings are typical of lithium toxicity?
options: Diffuse slowing, sometimes triphasic waves and sharp waves
questions.explanation: Lithium can slow the background even at therapeutic levels and may accentuate epileptiform activity. Toxicity causes diffuse slowing, triphasic waves, sharp waves and sometimes seizures, often with tremor, ataxia and confusion. Toxicity can occur even with levels in the reported range.
questions.memoryAid: LITHIUM LIGHTS UP the EEG: SLOWING, SHARPS and TRIPHASICS when toxic.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which antipsychotic has the highest risk of dose-dependent seizures and epileptiform discharges?
questions.explanation: Clozapine has the highest seizure risk of the antipsychotics, rising with dose. It commonly causes EEG slowing and epileptiform discharges. Phenothiazines such as chlorpromazine also lower the seizure threshold. High-potency drugs such as haloperidol carry a lower seizure risk.
questions.memoryAid: CLOZAPINE = 'CLOSE to a seizure'. Higher dose, closer it gets.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: An elderly patient with kidney failure on cefepime becomes confused. The EEG shows generalized triphasic-like periodic discharges. What should be considered?
questions.explanation: Cefepime (and other beta-lactams) can cause encephalopathy, myoclonus and non-convulsive status epilepticus, especially when kidney function is impaired and the drug accumulates. The EEG may show triphasic waves or generalized periodic discharges. Stopping the drug or adjusting the dose (sometimes dialysis) reverses it.
questions.memoryAid: CEFEPIME + KIDNEYS failing = CONFUSION and periodic discharges. 'Cefe-pime Piles up.'
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which drug used for sedation in intensive care produces beta activity at low doses and burst suppression at high doses, and can cause myoclonus?
questions.explanation: Propofol, a GABA-ergic anaesthetic, produces beta at low doses, slowing at moderate doses, and burst suppression or suppression at high doses. It is used for refractory status epilepticus. Involuntary movements and myoclonus can occur, especially at induction and emergence.
questions.memoryAid: PROPOFOL: the same staircase as barbiturates: BETA → SLOW → BURST suppression.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What effect does acute alcohol intoxication have on the waking EEG?
options: Slowing of the alpha rhythm and increased theta
questions.explanation: Acute alcohol slows the posterior rhythm and increases theta, with more slowing at higher levels; very high levels can cause coma. In withdrawal, seizures and photoparoxysmal responses can appear.
questions.memoryAid: ALCOHOL makes the brain SLOW (on the way in) and FIRE (on the way out, withdrawal).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What do cocaine and amphetamines typically do to the EEG and seizure risk?
options: Increase fast activity and raise the risk of seizures
Cause triphasic waves at usual doses
questions.explanation: Stimulants such as cocaine and amphetamines increase arousal with more beta and less slow activity, and they lower the seizure threshold. Cocaine can also cause stroke and vasospasm, leading to focal abnormalities.
questions.memoryAid: STIMULANTS SPEED the EEG and can SPARK seizures (and strokes).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Flumazenil is given to reverse a benzodiazepine overdose in a patient on long-term benzodiazepines. What is the main risk?
questions.explanation: Flumazenil competitively blocks benzodiazepine receptors. In people on long-term benzodiazepines, or who have taken a seizure-provoking co-ingestant such as a tricyclic, it can precipitate withdrawal and seizures.
questions.memoryAid: FLUMAZENIL FLIPS the brake OFF: sudden withdrawal → seizures.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How do benzodiazepines change sleep architecture?
options: Increase spindle-range activity, reduce slow-wave sleep and REM
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines increase spindle-like (sigma and beta) activity, shorten sleep latency, and reduce slow-wave sleep (N3) and REM. This matters when staging sleep in a sedated patient and when judging a reduced N3.
questions.memoryAid: BENZOS: MORE spindles, LESS deep sleep and dreams.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Many antidepressants (SSRIs, tricyclics, MAO inhibitors) affect REM sleep in which way?
options: They have no effect on REM
They create sleep-onset REM in everyone
They suppress REM; stopping them can cause REM rebound
questions.explanation: Most antidepressants suppress REM sleep and lengthen REM latency. When they are stopped, REM rebound can follow, with early REM periods that could be confused with narcolepsy. Medication history is essential when interpreting a sleep-onset REM period. Bupropion, trazodone and mirtazapine suppress REM little or not at all.
questions.memoryAid: ANTIDEPRESSANTS ANNUL REM; stop them and REM RETURNS early.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which EEG change is typical of antihistamines such as diphenhydramine?
options: Drowsiness and slowing; overdose can cause seizures, especially in children
questions.explanation: Sedating antihistamines produce drowsiness and EEG changes of drowsiness and sleep. Children can react paradoxically with excitation. Overdose can cause seizures, delirium and anticholinergic signs.
questions.memoryAid: ANTIHISTAMINE: SLEEPY usually, SEIZURES in overdose, WILD in some kids.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient on theophylline with high blood levels develops seizures. Why?
options: Theophylline lowers the seizure threshold; toxicity can cause seizures and status
questions.explanation: Theophylline (a methylxanthine like caffeine) is an adenosine antagonist that lowers the seizure threshold. Toxicity causes tremor, arrhythmias and seizures that can be difficult to control.
questions.memoryAid: THEOPHYLLINE = 'THE-O-FILL-up-on-caffeine': too much and the brain over-fires.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In an epilepsy monitoring unit, why are antiepileptic drugs often tapered?
options: To increase the chance of recording the patient's typical seizures
questions.explanation: Reducing antiepileptic drugs under supervision increases the likelihood of capturing habitual seizures for diagnosis or surgical localisation. It raises the risk of clusters, generalized seizures and status epilepticus, so seizure precautions and a rescue plan are essential.
questions.memoryAid: TAPER to CAPTURE, but have the RESCUE ready.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: As the dose of a GABA-ergic sedative such as propofol or pentobarbital is raised, which sequence of EEG changes is expected?
options: Increased beta, then slowing, then burst suppression, then suppression
Increased alpha, then 3 Hz spike-and-wave, then hypsarrhythmia
Slowing first, then increased beta, then burst suppression
Burst suppression first, then beta as the dose rises further
questions.explanation: GABA-ergic sedatives (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, propofol) follow a predictable staircase with rising dose: increased beta, then drowsiness and slowing, then burst suppression and finally suppression. Recognising the staircase helps you judge sedation depth.
questions.memoryAid: The SEDATIVE STAIRCASE: BETA → SLOW → BURSTS → FLAT.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which drug is classically avoided in Dravet syndrome because it can worsen seizures?
questions.explanation: Sodium channel blockers (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) can worsen seizures in Dravet syndrome, which is usually caused by loss-of-function SCN1A (sodium channel) variants. Valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine and cannabidiol are used.
questions.memoryAid: DRAVET: 'DON'T block the sodium'. Valproate and Clobazam are the 'VC' (very common) choices.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What does intravenous lorazepam do to ongoing generalized spike-and-wave in non-convulsive status?
options: It always converts them to triphasic waves
It usually abolishes the discharges, and clinical improvement supports the diagnosis
questions.explanation: A benzodiazepine trial during suspected non-convulsive status: resolution of the discharges together with clinical improvement supports NCSE. EEG improvement without clinical improvement is less conclusive, because benzodiazepines can also abolish triphasic waves in metabolic encephalopathy.
questions.memoryAid: BENZO TRIAL: EEG better AND patient better = it was a SEIZURE. EEG better alone = maybe not.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A patient on lithium has tremor, confusion, a 6 Hz posterior rhythm and diffuse theta with occasional triphasic waves. The lithium level is high. After lithium is stopped, what is the expected EEG course?
options: Gradual improvement of the slowing, which may lag days behind the fall in serum level
Permanent slowing, because drug effects on the EEG never reverse
Immediate normalisation the moment the serum level falls
questions.explanation: Lithium toxicity causes diffuse slowing, triphasic and sharp waves. These are reversible, but brain lithium clears more slowly than serum lithium, so EEG and clinical recovery can lag the serum level by days. Toxicity can also occur within the reported therapeutic range.
questions.memoryAid: LITHIUM LINGERS: the brain clears it LATER than the blood, so the EEG recovers LATE.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which drug can cause a reversible pattern that mimics electrocerebral inactivity in hypothermic overdose patients?
questions.explanation: Barbiturates at high levels, especially with hypothermia, can suppress the EEG completely, mimicking electrocerebral inactivity; this is reversible as levels fall. Hence the ACNS requirement to exclude drug intoxication and hypothermia before using EEG for brain death.
questions.memoryAid: PENTO-BARB + COLD = 'PRETEND flat'. Never confirm brain death until both are gone.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Under ACNS Guideline 1, what is the minimum number of recording channels for a routine EEG?
questions.explanation: Guideline 1 sets 16 channels as the minimum for routine EEG, using all 21 electrodes of the 10-20 System. Twelve cerebral channels is the neonatal minimum (Guideline 5); 21 is the number of electrodes, not channels.
questions.memoryAid: SIXTEEN to SEE it: 16 channels, 21 electrodes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: On the impedance check, one electrode reads 60 Ω. What does Guideline 1 suggest?
options: An acceptable value for routine EEG but not for ECI
Amplifier saturation that needs a lower sensitivity
An ideal contact that needs no action
A possible short or salt bridge; check the site
questions.explanation: Guideline 1 accepts impedances up to 10 kΩ but warns that a value below 100 Ω suggests a short circuit, usually a gel or salt bridge between neighbouring electrodes. Impedances should also be balanced across electrodes.
questions.memoryAid: Too LOW is a LEAK: under 100 Ω = salt bridge. Up to 10 kΩ is fine.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which filter settings meet Guideline 1 for a routine recording?
options: Low-frequency filter 0.1 Hz; high-frequency filter 15 Hz
Low-frequency filter no lower than 1 Hz; high-frequency filter no higher than 70 Hz
Low-frequency filter no higher than 1 Hz; high-frequency filter no lower than 70 Hz
Low-frequency filter 5 Hz; high-frequency filter 35 Hz
questions.explanation: Routine EEG must keep the bandwidth open: LFF no higher than 1 Hz (time constant at least 0.16 s) and HFF no lower than 70 Hz. Read the direction words carefully: 'no higher than' and 'no lower than' are limits in opposite directions. The 60 Hz notch is used only when other measures fail.
questions.memoryAid: ONE and SEVENTY, and keep the window WIDE: LFF ≤ 1, HFF ≥ 70.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which recording reference does Guideline 1 recommend for digital EEG?
options: An average of all scalp electrodes
An extra electrode between Cz and Pz
questions.explanation: Recording referentially lets every montage be rebuilt afterwards. The reference should be an extra electrode, commonly between Cz and Pz. Linked ears are specifically discouraged as the recording reference.
questions.memoryAid: The reference lives BETWEEN Cz and Pz, and the EARS are BANNED.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How long should hyperventilation last under Guideline 1, and how much recording follows it?
options: At least 3 minutes, with at least 1 minute of recording afterwards
At least 5 minutes, with 5 minutes afterwards
At least 1 minute, with no recording required afterwards
At least 2 minutes, with 30 seconds afterwards
questions.explanation: Guideline 1: HV for at least 3 min, with at least 1 min of baseline before and at least 1 min of recording after. Responses that persist after HV stops are clinically important, which is why the post-HV minute matters.
questions.memoryAid: HV 1-3-1: one minute before, THREE minutes of breathing, one minute after.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: When should photic stimulation be done relative to hyperventilation in an adult routine EEG?
options: Before HV, or 3 or more minutes after it
During HV, to save recording time
Straight after HV, while slowing persists
Only after a normal HV response
questions.explanation: Guideline 1 places the photic lamp at least 30 cm from the face and runs photic before HV or at least 3 min after it, so HV effects do not contaminate the photic response. (In children, Guideline 5 puts HV at the start and photic at the end.)
questions.memoryAid: Lights and breathing do not MIX: photic first, or wait 3 minutes.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What calibration does Guideline 1 require at the start of a digital recording?
options: A sine-wave sweep from 0.5 to 70 Hz
At least 10 seconds of square-wave calibration
No calibration, because digital systems are self-checking
questions.explanation: At least 10 s of square-wave calibration at the start. Biologic calibration is not needed for digital systems. Afterwards, review 30 s on the system reference montage without the notch filter.
questions.memoryAid: TEN seconds of SQUARES before you start.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: During a routine EEG the patient has an electrographic seizure. What does Guideline 1 expect of the technologist?
options: Explain the diagnosis to patient and family
Notify the reading physician and supervisor
Finish the study and leave it for the reader
Stop recording and start the next patient
questions.explanation: Guideline 1 makes the technologist responsible for notifying the interpreting physician and supervisor of critical results, including electrographic or clinical seizures and other significant clinical events. Interpreting or telling the family the diagnosis is outside the technologist's scope.
questions.memoryAid: CRITICAL = CALL: seizure seen, physician told.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How many montages should be viewed while recording under Guideline 1?
options: At least 3, both bipolar and referential
Every montage stored on the system
questions.explanation: View at least 3 montages during the recording, including at least one bipolar and one referential, and record both eyes open and eyes closed. Note state, stimuli, movements and patient effort.
questions.memoryAid: THREE views, both KINDS: bipolar AND referential.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In the 10-10 nomenclature (Guideline 2), what are the old T3 and T4 called?
questions.explanation: Guideline 2 renamed T3/T4 to T7/T8 and T5/T6 to P7/P8. The old names remain acceptable. P with a number of 7 or more marks a posterior temporal site; 6 or less is parietal.
questions.memoryAid: T3-T4 went up to SEVEN-EIGHT; T5-T6 moved to the P row.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which 10-10 positions closely approximate the anterior temporal T1 and T2 electrodes?
questions.explanation: FT9/FT10 closely approximate T1/T2. F9/F10, T9/T10 and P9/P10 sit 10% below the standard temporal row. The 10-10 system has more than 70 positions; the 10-5 system is not accepted by ACNS or IFCN.
questions.memoryAid: FT NINE = T ONE: 'Front-Temporal, low row'.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: A montage is labelled LB-16.2. What does that mean under Guideline 3?
options: A longitudinal bipolar montage with interelectrode distances of 2 cm
A 16-channel montage with a 2 µV/mm sensitivity
questions.explanation: The class (LB longitudinal bipolar, TB transverse bipolar, R referential) comes first; the number left of the point is the channel count and the number right of it is the alternative. There are no more than three alternatives per class and size.
questions.memoryAid: CLASS - CHANNELS . CHOICE: LB-16.2 = longitudinal, 16, option 2.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How does Guideline 3 order the channels on the display?
options: Midline first, then left, then right
Posterior above anterior, and right above left
In alphabetical order of electrode names
Anterior above posterior, and left above right
questions.explanation: Montages use simple straight chains with equal interelectrode distances, anterior above posterior and left above right, with each channel's derivation labelled and a single ECG channel. Each recording should include at least one montage of each class (LB, TB and R).
questions.memoryAid: Read it like a PAGE: top is the FRONT, LEFT comes first.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Temporal lobe epilepsy is suspected. Which referential choice does the guideline discussion favour?
options: An average reference that includes Fp1 and Fp2
Linked ears, since they balance both sides
Cz, since temporal fields often reach the ears
The ipsilateral ear, closest to the temporal lobe
questions.explanation: Temporal discharges often spread to A1/A2, so an ear reference becomes 'active' and distorts the picture. Cz is better here. Cz is a poor choice when sleep activity (vertex waves) is prominent; an ear reference suits a frontal focus. Average references often omit Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8 to limit eye artifact.
questions.memoryAid: TEMPORAL spike? The EAR hears it too, so go to the TOP (Cz).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the minimum sampling rate for digital EEG under Guideline 4?
questions.explanation: Guideline 4 sets at least 256 samples per second, with higher rates such as 512 preferable. Note the unit is samples per second, not Hz of bandwidth.
questions.memoryAid: TWO-FIVE-SIX to fix it in time; 512 is the nicer prize.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What analogue-to-digital resolution does Guideline 4 require?
questions.explanation: At least 16 bits per sample including the sign bit; most modern amplifiers use 24 bits.
questions.memoryAid: SIXTEEN channels, SIXTEEN bits.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the Guideline 4 minimum common mode rejection ratio for each channel?
questions.explanation: CMRR is a ratio expressed in dB, and the minimum is 90 dB per channel (higher is better). A common distractor gives it in Hz. Interchannel crosstalk must be under 1% (40 dB down) and added noise under 1 µV peak to peak from 0.5 to 100 Hz.
questions.memoryAid: CMRR is in DECIBELS: NINETY dB rejects the noise.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How large should one second be on screen, according to Guideline 4?
questions.explanation: One second should occupy 25 to 35 mm, mirroring the old 30 mm/s paper speed. The display also needs at least 10 mm per channel for up to 21 channels, scales shown on screen and a time stamp on every page.
questions.memoryAid: About THIRTY mm a second, just like the old paper.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which storage practice does Guideline 4 recommend?
options: A public format such as EDF/EDF+
Raw data deleted after the report
questions.explanation: Guideline 4 advises against optical discs, recommends server storage for inpatient studies of 24 h or more, and requires the ability to read and write a public format such as EDF/EDF+ with a stand-alone viewer. Impedances, filters, gain, montage and any changes are logged automatically.
questions.memoryAid: EDF = Everyone Can Read the File.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What low-frequency filter does Guideline 5 specify for neonatal EEG?
questions.explanation: Neonatal records contain important very slow activity, so the LFF is lowered to 0.3 to 0.6 Hz rather than the adult 1 Hz. Sensitivity is usually 7 µV/mm.
questions.memoryAid: BABIES are SLOW: drop the LFF to about 0.5 Hz.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of cerebral channels for a neonatal EEG under Guideline 5?
options: At least 8 cerebral channels with no polygraphy
At least 12 cerebral channels plus polygraphic channels
At least 16 cerebral channels with no polygraphy
questions.explanation: Neonates (up to 4 to 8 weeks post-term) need at least 12 cerebral channels plus at least 2 polygraphic channels (16 or more helps). A reduced array is allowed, Cz is always included, and needle electrodes are never used.
questions.memoryAid: TWELVE for the TINY, plus the POLY (ECG, breathing, eyes, chin).
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: How long should a neonatal EEG run when the pattern stays the same, under Guideline 5?
options: At least 60 min, with a full quiet-sleep epoch
At least 3 hours, with sedation for sleep
20 minutes, the same as an adult study
questions.explanation: 20 to 30 min is usually insufficient in neonates. Record at least 60 min if the pattern is invariant, including a full epoch of quiet sleep, and never sedate a neonate to obtain sleep. Photic stimulation is not recommended.
questions.memoryAid: An HOUR for a BABY, and catch QUIET sleep.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: In a child's routine EEG, how does Guideline 5 order the activations?
options: HV at the start, photic at the end
HV only once the child is asleep
Photic at the start, HV at the end
questions.explanation: Guideline 5 puts HV at the start and photic at the end for children; a second HV can follow at least 10 min after the first. Sensitivity may be reduced to 10 or 15 µV/mm when needed, with part run at about 7 µV/mm.
questions.memoryAid: Kids BREATHE first, FLASH last.
questions.author: NeuroLinea Focus Drills (AI-drafted, fact-checked; requires expert review)

questions.stem: Which age term does Guideline 5 use for neonates, following the American Academy of Pediatrics?
options: Postmenstrual age = gestational age + chronological age
